answer:
The exclusive platform referenced is **Arcade Island** (often abbreviated as **AI**), which is a featured gaming section within the **PCH+** app operated by **Publishers Clearing House (PCH)**.

Here is the breakdown based on the search results:
*   **The League:** Refers to the **NFL** (National Football League), specifically linked to the **Super Bowl** (whose halftime show is the iconic "halftime event" mentioned). PCH famously announced its $10 million sweepstakes winners just after the Super Bowl for decades.
*   **The Video Game/Game:** While there is no single video game strictly "named for the league" that dominates the description, PCH markets various games (including sports-themed ones or general arcade games) under its umbrella. The marketing highlights "exclusive games" available on the platform.
*   **The Platform:** The specific exclusive platform for these games is called **Arcade Island**.
*   **The Abbreviated Name:** The abbreviated name for **Arcade Island** is **AI**. (Alternatively, the overarching app is often referred to by its abbreviation **PCH+**, but "Arcade Island" is the specific game platform name).

Answer: **AI** (for **Arcade Island**)

**Publishers Clearing House** (**PCH**) is an American company founded in 1953 by Harold Mertz. The company offered bulk maildirect marketing of periodicals (and later merchandise) as an alternative to door-to-door magazine subscription sales. Publishers Clearing House is most widely known for its sweepstakes and prize-based games, which were introduced in 1967. From August 2020 to March 2024, it owned the Wide Open Media publications _Wide Open Spaces_ (about outdoorslifestyle), _Wide Open Country_ (about country music), and _FanBuzz_ (about sports).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Criteo-4)

PCH sweepstakes have been subject to legal action regarding whether consumers were misled about the odds of winning, and whether purchases improved their chances. By 2010, the company had reached settlements with all 50 states, and in 2023 the Federal Trade Commission ordered PCH to overhaul its sweepstakes processes.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-ftc-5) In 2025, PCH filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection and its assets were acquired by ARB Interactive, an online sweepstakes company.
Publishers Clearing House was founded in 1953 in Port Washington, New York by Harold Mertz,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-llp-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Saslow-7) a former manager of a door-to-door sales team for magazine subscriptions.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-ten-8) The company started in Mertz's basement with help from his first wife LuEsther and daughter Joyce.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-resp-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-book-10) Its first mailings were of 10,000 envelopes from Mertz's home on Long Island, New York, and offered 20 magazine subscriptions. A hundred orders were received. Within a few years, the company moved out of Mertz's basement into an office building and started hiring staff. When PCH moved its headquarters in 1969, its prior location was donated to the city and renamed the Harold E. Mertz Community Center.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-book-10) The company's revenue had grown to US$50 million by 1981, and $100 million by 1988.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-ten-8)

In 1967, PCH ran its first sweepstakes as a way to increase subscription sales,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-two-11) modeled after sweepstakes held by _[Reader's Digest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reader's\_Digest "Reader's Digest")_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-llp-6) The first prizes ranged from $1 to $10 and entrants had a 1 in 10 chance of winning. After the sweepstakes increased response rates to mailings, prizes of $5,000[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-ten-8) and eventually $250,000 were offered.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-wsj-12) PCH began advertising the sweepstakes on TV in 1974.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-resp-9)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-eight-13) It was the only major multi-magazine subscription business until 1977. Former client [Time Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Inc. "Time Inc.") and several other publishers formed American Family Publishers (AFP) to compete with PCH after the company refused repeated requests by Time for a larger share of sales revenue from magazine subscriptions.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-llp-6)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-book-10)

AFP and PCH competed for exclusive rights to magazines and for the better promotion and prize ideas. When AFP increased its jackpot to $1 million,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-wsj-12) and then to $10 million in 1985, PCH raised its prizes to match.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-llp-6) PCH had distributed $7 million in prizes by 1979,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-14) $40 million by 1991,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Saslow-7) and $137 million by 2000.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-two-11) In 1989, two members of its advertising team, Dave Sayer and Todd Sloane, started the Prize Patrol, a publicized event where winners are surprised with a check at their home. The idea was inspired by the 1950s television series _The Millionaire_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-llp-6)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-five-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-16) The two companies were often mistaken for each other, with AFP spokespeopleEd McMahon and Dick Clark mistaken for representatives of the better-known PCH.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Forbes-17)

### Government regulation and legal actions
[edit]
Beginning in the 1990s, PCH and its primary competitor, AFP, experienced a series of lawsuits claiming that their mailings misled consumers about their odds of winning and implied that magazine purchases improved their chances.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-llp-6)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-wsj-12) This led to the Deceptive Mail Prevention and Enforcement Act of 2000, which regulates direct mail businesses.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-llp-6) At the Senate hearings regarding this Act, PCH claimed most consumers were not confused about their chances of winning or that purchases did not increase their chances. The company said that fewer than five percent of participants spent more than $300.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-book-10) However, government officials from California claimed 5,000 local consumers spent more than $2,500 each in magazine purchases under the false belief that they were increasing their odds of winning the sweepstakes.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-opyltwo-18)
Industry sources estimated that PCH's response rates decreased by 7 to 12 percent and its sales volume by 22 to 30 percent in response to negative publicity from these lawsuits.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-ten-8)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-libn.com-19) In 2000, PCH laid off a quarter of its 800-person workforce.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-libn.com-19)

### Government regulation and legal actions
#### Lawsuits and settlements
[edit]
In 1992, thousands of discarded sweepstakes entries from contestants who had not bought magazine subscriptions were found in the company's trash, reinforcing beliefs that the company favored those who made purchases in selecting a sweepstakes winner.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-llp-6) PCH said this was done by a disgruntled employee at its mail processing vendor.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-book-10) A class action lawsuit ensued, which PCH settled by giving discarded entrants a second chance to win.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-llp-6)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-20)
In 1994, PCH sent mailings telling recipients they were all "finalists", which led to[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-wsj-12) a lawsuit involving the attorneys general of 14 US states.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-one-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-23) Later that year, PCH denied wrongdoing, but agreed to pay a settlement of $490,000 and to change its practices.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-one-22) Under the agreement, PCH said it would define terms like "finalist" and disclose the chances of winning.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-24)

### Government regulation and legal actions
#### Lawsuits and settlements
In 1997, a contestant of competitor AFP flew to Tampa, Florida, thinking he had won, though he had not. The resulting publicity caused more lawsuits for both companies.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-ten-8) PCH reached a $30 million national settlement in 1999.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-book-10)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-25) In 2000, another $18 million settlement was reached with 24 states, after the company sent mass mailings which said "You are a winner!" and used mock personalized checks.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-opyltwo-18)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-opyl-26) PCH agreed to avoid similar mailings in the future, and add a "sweepstakes fact box" to mailings.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-opyltwo-18)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-opyl-26)

### Government regulation and legal actions
#### Lawsuits and settlements
Concerns about deceptive practices by PCH continued after this national settlement and the passing of the Deceptive Mail Prevention and Enforcement Act in 2000. State attorneys spoke out against the national settlement, and individual states filed additional lawsuits.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-book-10) Another $34 million settlement was reached in 2001 in a lawsuit involving 25 states, bringing the total settlements since 1999 to $82 million.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Clifford-1)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-six-27) As part of the settlement, PCH was required to avoid terms including "Guaranteed Winner," and to add disclaimers to mailings saying that the recipient had not yet won and that purchasing merchandise would not improve the chances of winning.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-seven-28)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-six-27)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Ulferts-29) PCH reached settlements with all 50 states and agreed to work with a "compliance counsel."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-ten-8) PCH apologized in the settlement and said it would contact customers who had spent more than $1,000 on merchandise the prior year.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Ulferts-29)

### Government regulation and legal actions
#### Lawsuits and settlements
PCH reached another agreement with Iowa in 2007.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-30) In 2010, the company paid $3.5 million to the attorneys general of 32 states and the [District of Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") to settle possible contempt charges that it had violated the terms of the 2001 agreement. The company denied wrongdoing, but agreed to work with both an ombudsman and a compliance counsel who would review its mailings quarterly.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Pankratz-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-34)
In April 2014, an investigation by the Senate Special Committee on Aging concluded that PCH had "pushed the limits" of federal law and legal settlements and that additional legislation might be needed, especially since the 2000 law did not cover email and other online communications.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-35)
Beginning in late 2021, PCH was hit with multiple new class action lawsuits, alleging that "Publishers Clearing House sells and rents mailing lists containing subscribers' personal information to a variety of third parties ... with each claiming the publishing company monetizes its subscribers' private information—including their names and addresses—without consent."[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-37)

### Government regulation and legal actions
#### Lawsuits and settlements
In June 2023, the Federal Trade Commission ordered PCH "to overhaul its sweepstakes entry and sales processes, stop surprise fees, and pay $18.5 million to consumers."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-ftc-5) At that time, the FTC also issued a consumer alert describing the deceptive practices in which PCH was found to engage.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-38)
Beginning in the 1990s, the company shifted its focus online.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Clifford-1)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-39) It began selling magazine subscriptions and merchandise on PCH.com in 1996.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Levere-40) PCH acquired the assets of search company Blingo in 2006,[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-41) online gaming company Funtank in 2010, mobile marketing company Liquid Wireless in 2012, and internet news aggregator Topix in 2019.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-42)

### Wide Open Media publishing
The company's initial product was magazine subscriptions sold at a discount.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-four-53) Industry experts estimated that companies like PCH kept 75 to 90 percent of the fees from the original subscription, while publishers used the increased distribution to improve circulation numbers and revenue from renewals.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-wsj-12)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-54) PCH popularized the idea of using sweepstakes to sell magazine subscriptions through direct marketing, and became known by detractors as a producer of junk mail for advertising through mass-mailings.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Saslow-7)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-four-53) Documents filed with the New York Department of State in 1993 said that year the company mailed 220 million envelopes. Frequent buyers received 30 to 40 mailings a year.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-nine-55)
PCH began selling merchandise in 1985 with two products.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-resp-9) After a Hershey's Chocolate Cookbook and a diet cookbook sold more than other products, the company began expanding into jewelry, media, collectibles, household products, and others.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-book-10)

### Wide Open Media publishing
By the mid-2000's, the majority of the company's revenue came from merchandise sales.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-eight-13) As late as 2019, PCH operated eight websites, including PCH Search and Win, PCH Lotto, PCH Games, PCH Save and Win, and Candystand.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Clifford-1)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-eight-13)
In 2024, direct mail and product sales were discontinued.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-57)
The Prize Patrol delivering an oversized check in 2011 to a sweepstakes winner for $1 million plus $5,000 a week for life

### Wide Open Media publishing
In 1995, PCH began the tradition of announcing winners of its $10 million prize just after the Super Bowl.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Meier-58) By the time of its bankruptcy in 2025, the company had distributed more than $500 million in prizes.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-AP-BK-2) Some of its larger prizes have been for $5,000 a week for life,[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-59) or for $10 million.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-about-60) Prizes can also range from $1 Amazon gift cards to $2,500, $1 million or $3 million.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-primary-61) The larger cash prizes are paid in installments, typically with a balloon payment at 30 years,[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-62) reducing the present value of prizes to much less than their nominal values. In August 2024, "early look" prizes were eliminated.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-63) The odds of winning "$5,000 a Week for Life" were 1 in 6.2 billion.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-64)

### Wide Open Media publishing
The Prize Patrol surprises sweepstakes winners with oversized checks for $1,000 to $10 million at their homes, workplaces, or other locations, capturing the event on video. Since their introduction in 1989, these videos have been used in widely broadcast television commercials, and, more recently, in the company's online acquisition efforts, websites and social media communications.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-resp-9)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-eight-13)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-seven-28)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-NYTTYN-65) In 2013, a $5 million television campaign modified the traditional prize patrol commercial by digitally altering video from classic sitcoms like _The Brady Bunch_ and _[Gilligan's Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilligan's\_Island "Gilligan's Island")_ to show the prize patrol visiting characters in the show.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-NYTTYN-65) Major winners are never contacted in advance; any letters, telephone calls, and social media messages claiming that a person may have already won a major prize, or claiming that they need to pay a fee to collect the prize, are always scams.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-66)

### Wide Open Media publishing
The Prize Patrol has made in-person appearances or delivered prizes on TV programs including _The Oprah Winfrey Show_,[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-67)_The Price Is Right_,[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-69) and _[Let's Make a Deal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Let's\_Make\_a\_Deal "Let's Make a Deal")_. Their surprise winning moments have been spoofed by Jay Leno,[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-70)[Conan O'Brien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conan_O'Brien "Conan O'Brien"),[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-71) and the cast of _Saturday Night Live_;[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-72) woven into the plots of movies such as _[Let's Go to Prison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Let's\_Go\_to\_Prison "Let's Go to Prison")_,[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-74)_The Sentinel_,[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-75) and _Knight and Day_;[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-76)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-77) and the TV series _Early Edition_. They have been the subject of cartoons.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-book-10)

**Publishers Clearing House** (**PCH**) is an American company founded in 1953 by Harold Mertz. The company offered bulk maildirect marketing of periodicals (and later merchandise) as an alternative to door-to-door magazine subscription sales. Publishers Clearing House is most widely known for its sweepstakes and prize-based games, which were introduced in 1967. From August 2020 to March 2024, it owned the Wide Open Media publications _Wide Open Spaces_ (about outdoorslifestyle), _Wide Open Country_ (about country music), and _FanBuzz_ (about sports).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Criteo-4)
texts.1:
PCH sweepstakes have been subject to legal action regarding whether consumers were misled about the odds of winning, and whether purchases improved their chances. By 2010, the company had reached settlements with all 50 states, and in 2023 the Federal Trade Commission ordered PCH to overhaul its sweepstakes processes.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-ftc-5) In 2025, PCH filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection and its assets were acquired by ARB Interactive, an online sweepstakes company.
Publishers Clearing House was founded in 1953 in Port Washington, New York by Harold Mertz,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-llp-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Saslow-7) a former manager of a door-to-door sales team for magazine subscriptions.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-ten-8) The company started in Mertz's basement with help from his first wife LuEsther and daughter Joyce.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-resp-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-book-10) Its first mailings were of 10,000 envelopes from Mertz's home on Long Island, New York, and offered 20 magazine subscriptions. A hundred orders were received. Within a few years, the company moved out of Mertz's basement into an office building and started hiring staff. When PCH moved its headquarters in 1969, its prior location was donated to the city and renamed the Harold E. Mertz Community Center.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-book-10) The company's revenue had grown to US$50 million by 1981, and $100 million by 1988.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-ten-8)
texts.2: In 1967, PCH ran its first sweepstakes as a way to increase subscription sales,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-two-11) modeled after sweepstakes held by _[Reader's Digest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reader's\_Digest "Reader's Digest")_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-llp-6) The first prizes ranged from $1 to $10 and entrants had a 1 in 10 chance of winning. After the sweepstakes increased response rates to mailings, prizes of $5,000[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-ten-8) and eventually $250,000 were offered.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-wsj-12) PCH began advertising the sweepstakes on TV in 1974.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-resp-9)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-eight-13) It was the only major multi-magazine subscription business until 1977. Former client [Time Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Inc. "Time Inc.") and several other publishers formed American Family Publishers (AFP) to compete with PCH after the company refused repeated requests by Time for a larger share of sales revenue from magazine subscriptions.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-llp-6)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-book-10)
texts.3: AFP and PCH competed for exclusive rights to magazines and for the better promotion and prize ideas. When AFP increased its jackpot to $1 million,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-wsj-12) and then to $10 million in 1985, PCH raised its prizes to match.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-llp-6) PCH had distributed $7 million in prizes by 1979,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-14) $40 million by 1991,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Saslow-7) and $137 million by 2000.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-two-11) In 1989, two members of its advertising team, Dave Sayer and Todd Sloane, started the Prize Patrol, a publicized event where winners are surprised with a check at their home. The idea was inspired by the 1950s television series _The Millionaire_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-llp-6)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-five-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-16) The two companies were often mistaken for each other, with AFP spokespeopleEd McMahon and Dick Clark mistaken for representatives of the better-known PCH.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Forbes-17)
texts.4:
### Government regulation and legal actions
[edit]
Beginning in the 1990s, PCH and its primary competitor, AFP, experienced a series of lawsuits claiming that their mailings misled consumers about their odds of winning and implied that magazine purchases improved their chances.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-llp-6)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-wsj-12) This led to the Deceptive Mail Prevention and Enforcement Act of 2000, which regulates direct mail businesses.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-llp-6) At the Senate hearings regarding this Act, PCH claimed most consumers were not confused about their chances of winning or that purchases did not increase their chances. The company said that fewer than five percent of participants spent more than $300.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-book-10) However, government officials from California claimed 5,000 local consumers spent more than $2,500 each in magazine purchases under the false belief that they were increasing their odds of winning the sweepstakes.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-opyltwo-18)
Industry sources estimated that PCH's response rates decreased by 7 to 12 percent and its sales volume by 22 to 30 percent in response to negative publicity from these lawsuits.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-ten-8)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-libn.com-19) In 2000, PCH laid off a quarter of its 800-person workforce.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-libn.com-19)
texts.5:
### Government regulation and legal actions
#### Lawsuits and settlements
[edit]
In 1992, thousands of discarded sweepstakes entries from contestants who had not bought magazine subscriptions were found in the company's trash, reinforcing beliefs that the company favored those who made purchases in selecting a sweepstakes winner.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-llp-6) PCH said this was done by a disgruntled employee at its mail processing vendor.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-book-10) A class action lawsuit ensued, which PCH settled by giving discarded entrants a second chance to win.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-llp-6)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-20)
In 1994, PCH sent mailings telling recipients they were all "finalists", which led to[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-wsj-12) a lawsuit involving the attorneys general of 14 US states.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-one-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-23) Later that year, PCH denied wrongdoing, but agreed to pay a settlement of $490,000 and to change its practices.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-one-22) Under the agreement, PCH said it would define terms like "finalist" and disclose the chances of winning.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-24)
texts.6:
### Government regulation and legal actions
#### Lawsuits and settlements
In 1997, a contestant of competitor AFP flew to Tampa, Florida, thinking he had won, though he had not. The resulting publicity caused more lawsuits for both companies.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-ten-8) PCH reached a $30 million national settlement in 1999.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-book-10)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-25) In 2000, another $18 million settlement was reached with 24 states, after the company sent mass mailings which said "You are a winner!" and used mock personalized checks.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-opyltwo-18)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-opyl-26) PCH agreed to avoid similar mailings in the future, and add a "sweepstakes fact box" to mailings.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-opyltwo-18)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-opyl-26)
texts.7:
### Government regulation and legal actions
#### Lawsuits and settlements
Concerns about deceptive practices by PCH continued after this national settlement and the passing of the Deceptive Mail Prevention and Enforcement Act in 2000. State attorneys spoke out against the national settlement, and individual states filed additional lawsuits.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-book-10) Another $34 million settlement was reached in 2001 in a lawsuit involving 25 states, bringing the total settlements since 1999 to $82 million.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Clifford-1)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-six-27) As part of the settlement, PCH was required to avoid terms including "Guaranteed Winner," and to add disclaimers to mailings saying that the recipient had not yet won and that purchasing merchandise would not improve the chances of winning.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-seven-28)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-six-27)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Ulferts-29) PCH reached settlements with all 50 states and agreed to work with a "compliance counsel."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-ten-8) PCH apologized in the settlement and said it would contact customers who had spent more than $1,000 on merchandise the prior year.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Ulferts-29)
texts.8:
### Government regulation and legal actions
#### Lawsuits and settlements
PCH reached another agreement with Iowa in 2007.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-30) In 2010, the company paid $3.5 million to the attorneys general of 32 states and the [District of Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") to settle possible contempt charges that it had violated the terms of the 2001 agreement. The company denied wrongdoing, but agreed to work with both an ombudsman and a compliance counsel who would review its mailings quarterly.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Pankratz-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-34)
In April 2014, an investigation by the Senate Special Committee on Aging concluded that PCH had "pushed the limits" of federal law and legal settlements and that additional legislation might be needed, especially since the 2000 law did not cover email and other online communications.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-35)
Beginning in late 2021, PCH was hit with multiple new class action lawsuits, alleging that "Publishers Clearing House sells and rents mailing lists containing subscribers' personal information to a variety of third parties ... with each claiming the publishing company monetizes its subscribers' private information—including their names and addresses—without consent."[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-37)
texts.9:
### Government regulation and legal actions
#### Lawsuits and settlements
In June 2023, the Federal Trade Commission ordered PCH "to overhaul its sweepstakes entry and sales processes, stop surprise fees, and pay $18.5 million to consumers."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-ftc-5) At that time, the FTC also issued a consumer alert describing the deceptive practices in which PCH was found to engage.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-38)
Beginning in the 1990s, the company shifted its focus online.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Clifford-1)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-39) It began selling magazine subscriptions and merchandise on PCH.com in 1996.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Levere-40) PCH acquired the assets of search company Blingo in 2006,[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-41) online gaming company Funtank in 2010, mobile marketing company Liquid Wireless in 2012, and internet news aggregator Topix in 2019.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-42)
texts.13:
### Wide Open Media publishing
The company's initial product was magazine subscriptions sold at a discount.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-four-53) Industry experts estimated that companies like PCH kept 75 to 90 percent of the fees from the original subscription, while publishers used the increased distribution to improve circulation numbers and revenue from renewals.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-wsj-12)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-54) PCH popularized the idea of using sweepstakes to sell magazine subscriptions through direct marketing, and became known by detractors as a producer of junk mail for advertising through mass-mailings.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Saslow-7)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-four-53) Documents filed with the New York Department of State in 1993 said that year the company mailed 220 million envelopes. Frequent buyers received 30 to 40 mailings a year.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-nine-55)
PCH began selling merchandise in 1985 with two products.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-resp-9) After a Hershey's Chocolate Cookbook and a diet cookbook sold more than other products, the company began expanding into jewelry, media, collectibles, household products, and others.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-book-10)
texts.14:
### Wide Open Media publishing
By the mid-2000's, the majority of the company's revenue came from merchandise sales.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-eight-13) As late as 2019, PCH operated eight websites, including PCH Search and Win, PCH Lotto, PCH Games, PCH Save and Win, and Candystand.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Clifford-1)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-eight-13)
In 2024, direct mail and product sales were discontinued.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-57)
The Prize Patrol delivering an oversized check in 2011 to a sweepstakes winner for $1 million plus $5,000 a week for life
texts.15:
### Wide Open Media publishing
In 1995, PCH began the tradition of announcing winners of its $10 million prize just after the Super Bowl.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Meier-58) By the time of its bankruptcy in 2025, the company had distributed more than $500 million in prizes.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-AP-BK-2) Some of its larger prizes have been for $5,000 a week for life,[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-59) or for $10 million.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-about-60) Prizes can also range from $1 Amazon gift cards to $2,500, $1 million or $3 million.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-primary-61) The larger cash prizes are paid in installments, typically with a balloon payment at 30 years,[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-62) reducing the present value of prizes to much less than their nominal values. In August 2024, "early look" prizes were eliminated.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-63) The odds of winning "$5,000 a Week for Life" were 1 in 6.2 billion.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-64)
texts.16:
### Wide Open Media publishing
The Prize Patrol surprises sweepstakes winners with oversized checks for $1,000 to $10 million at their homes, workplaces, or other locations, capturing the event on video. Since their introduction in 1989, these videos have been used in widely broadcast television commercials, and, more recently, in the company's online acquisition efforts, websites and social media communications.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-resp-9)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-eight-13)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-seven-28)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-NYTTYN-65) In 2013, a $5 million television campaign modified the traditional prize patrol commercial by digitally altering video from classic sitcoms like _The Brady Bunch_ and _[Gilligan's Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilligan's\_Island "Gilligan's Island")_ to show the prize patrol visiting characters in the show.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-NYTTYN-65) Major winners are never contacted in advance; any letters, telephone calls, and social media messages claiming that a person may have already won a major prize, or claiming that they need to pay a fee to collect the prize, are always scams.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-66)
texts.17:
### Wide Open Media publishing
The Prize Patrol has made in-person appearances or delivered prizes on TV programs including _The Oprah Winfrey Show_,[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-67)_The Price Is Right_,[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-69) and _[Let's Make a Deal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Let's\_Make\_a\_Deal "Let's Make a Deal")_. Their surprise winning moments have been spoofed by Jay Leno,[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-70)[Conan O'Brien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conan_O'Brien "Conan O'Brien"),[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-71) and the cast of _Saturday Night Live_;[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-72) woven into the plots of movies such as _[Let's Go to Prison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Let's\_Go\_to\_Prison "Let's Go to Prison")_,[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-74)_The Sentinel_,[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-75) and _Knight and Day_;[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-76)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-77) and the TV series _Early Edition_. They have been the subject of cartoons.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-book-10)

Publishers Clearing House was founded in 1953 in Port Washington, New York by Harold Mertz,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-llp-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Saslow-7) a former manager of a door-to-door sales team for magazine subscriptions.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-ten-8) The company started in Mertz's basement with help from his first wife LuEsther and daughter Joyce.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-resp-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-book-10) Its first mailings were of 10,000 envelopes from Mertz's home on Long Island, New York, and offered 20 magazine subscriptions. A hundred orders were received. Within a few years, the company moved out of Mertz's basement into an office building and started hiring staff. When PCH moved its headquarters in 1969, its prior location was donated to the city and renamed the Harold E. Mertz Community Center.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-book-10) The company's revenue had grown to US$50 million by 1981, and $100 million by 1988.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-ten-8)

In 1967, PCH ran its first sweepstakes as a way to increase subscription sales,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-two-11) modeled after sweepstakes held by _[Reader's Digest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reader's\_Digest "Reader's Digest")_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-llp-6) The first prizes ranged from $1 to $10 and entrants had a 1 in 10 chance of winning. After the sweepstakes increased response rates to mailings, prizes of $5,000[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-ten-8) and eventually $250,000 were offered.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-wsj-12) PCH began advertising the sweepstakes on TV in 1974.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-resp-9)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-eight-13) It was the only major multi-magazine subscription business until 1977. Former client [Time Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Inc. "Time Inc.") and several other publishers formed American Family Publishers (AFP) to compete with PCH after the company refused repeated requests by Time for a larger share of sales revenue from magazine subscriptions.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-llp-6)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-book-10)

AFP and PCH competed for exclusive rights to magazines and for the better promotion and prize ideas. When AFP increased its jackpot to $1 million,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-wsj-12) and then to $10 million in 1985, PCH raised its prizes to match.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-llp-6) PCH had distributed $7 million in prizes by 1979,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-14) $40 million by 1991,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Saslow-7) and $137 million by 2000.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-two-11) In 1989, two members of its advertising team, Dave Sayer and Todd Sloane, started the Prize Patrol, a publicized event where winners are surprised with a check at their home. The idea was inspired by the 1950s television series _The Millionaire_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-llp-6)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-five-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-16) The two companies were often mistaken for each other, with AFP spokespeopleEd McMahon and Dick Clark mistaken for representatives of the better-known PCH.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Forbes-17)

### Government regulation and legal actions
[edit]
Beginning in the 1990s, PCH and its primary competitor, AFP, experienced a series of lawsuits claiming that their mailings misled consumers about their odds of winning and implied that magazine purchases improved their chances.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-llp-6)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-wsj-12) This led to the Deceptive Mail Prevention and Enforcement Act of 2000, which regulates direct mail businesses.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-llp-6) At the Senate hearings regarding this Act, PCH claimed most consumers were not confused about their chances of winning or that purchases did not increase their chances. The company said that fewer than five percent of participants spent more than $300.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-book-10) However, government officials from California claimed 5,000 local consumers spent more than $2,500 each in magazine purchases under the false belief that they were increasing their odds of winning the sweepstakes.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-opyltwo-18)
Industry sources estimated that PCH's response rates decreased by 7 to 12 percent and its sales volume by 22 to 30 percent in response to negative publicity from these lawsuits.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-ten-8)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-libn.com-19) In 2000, PCH laid off a quarter of its 800-person workforce.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-libn.com-19)

### Government regulation and legal actions
#### Lawsuits and settlements
[edit]
In 1992, thousands of discarded sweepstakes entries from contestants who had not bought magazine subscriptions were found in the company's trash, reinforcing beliefs that the company favored those who made purchases in selecting a sweepstakes winner.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-llp-6) PCH said this was done by a disgruntled employee at its mail processing vendor.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-book-10) A class action lawsuit ensued, which PCH settled by giving discarded entrants a second chance to win.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-llp-6)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-20)
In 1994, PCH sent mailings telling recipients they were all "finalists", which led to[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-wsj-12) a lawsuit involving the attorneys general of 14 US states.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-one-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-23) Later that year, PCH denied wrongdoing, but agreed to pay a settlement of $490,000 and to change its practices.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-one-22) Under the agreement, PCH said it would define terms like "finalist" and disclose the chances of winning.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-24)

### Government regulation and legal actions
#### Lawsuits and settlements
In 1997, a contestant of competitor AFP flew to Tampa, Florida, thinking he had won, though he had not. The resulting publicity caused more lawsuits for both companies.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-ten-8) PCH reached a $30 million national settlement in 1999.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-book-10)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-25) In 2000, another $18 million settlement was reached with 24 states, after the company sent mass mailings which said "You are a winner!" and used mock personalized checks.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-opyltwo-18)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-opyl-26) PCH agreed to avoid similar mailings in the future, and add a "sweepstakes fact box" to mailings.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-opyltwo-18)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-opyl-26)

### Government regulation and legal actions
#### Lawsuits and settlements
Concerns about deceptive practices by PCH continued after this national settlement and the passing of the Deceptive Mail Prevention and Enforcement Act in 2000. State attorneys spoke out against the national settlement, and individual states filed additional lawsuits.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-book-10) Another $34 million settlement was reached in 2001 in a lawsuit involving 25 states, bringing the total settlements since 1999 to $82 million.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Clifford-1)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-six-27) As part of the settlement, PCH was required to avoid terms including "Guaranteed Winner," and to add disclaimers to mailings saying that the recipient had not yet won and that purchasing merchandise would not improve the chances of winning.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-seven-28)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-six-27)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Ulferts-29) PCH reached settlements with all 50 states and agreed to work with a "compliance counsel."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-ten-8) PCH apologized in the settlement and said it would contact customers who had spent more than $1,000 on merchandise the prior year.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Ulferts-29)

### Government regulation and legal actions
#### Lawsuits and settlements
PCH reached another agreement with Iowa in 2007.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-30) In 2010, the company paid $3.5 million to the attorneys general of 32 states and the [District of Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") to settle possible contempt charges that it had violated the terms of the 2001 agreement. The company denied wrongdoing, but agreed to work with both an ombudsman and a compliance counsel who would review its mailings quarterly.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Pankratz-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-34)
In April 2014, an investigation by the Senate Special Committee on Aging concluded that PCH had "pushed the limits" of federal law and legal settlements and that additional legislation might be needed, especially since the 2000 law did not cover email and other online communications.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-35)
Beginning in late 2021, PCH was hit with multiple new class action lawsuits, alleging that "Publishers Clearing House sells and rents mailing lists containing subscribers' personal information to a variety of third parties ... with each claiming the publishing company monetizes its subscribers' private information—including their names and addresses—without consent."[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-37)

### Government regulation and legal actions
#### Lawsuits and settlements
In June 2023, the Federal Trade Commission ordered PCH "to overhaul its sweepstakes entry and sales processes, stop surprise fees, and pay $18.5 million to consumers."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-ftc-5) At that time, the FTC also issued a consumer alert describing the deceptive practices in which PCH was found to engage.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-38)
Beginning in the 1990s, the company shifted its focus online.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Clifford-1)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-39) It began selling magazine subscriptions and merchandise on PCH.com in 1996.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Levere-40) PCH acquired the assets of search company Blingo in 2006,[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-41) online gaming company Funtank in 2010, mobile marketing company Liquid Wireless in 2012, and internet news aggregator Topix in 2019.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-42)

### Wide Open Media publishing
The company's initial product was magazine subscriptions sold at a discount.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-four-53) Industry experts estimated that companies like PCH kept 75 to 90 percent of the fees from the original subscription, while publishers used the increased distribution to improve circulation numbers and revenue from renewals.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-wsj-12)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-54) PCH popularized the idea of using sweepstakes to sell magazine subscriptions through direct marketing, and became known by detractors as a producer of junk mail for advertising through mass-mailings.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Saslow-7)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-four-53) Documents filed with the New York Department of State in 1993 said that year the company mailed 220 million envelopes. Frequent buyers received 30 to 40 mailings a year.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-nine-55)
PCH began selling merchandise in 1985 with two products.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-resp-9) After a Hershey's Chocolate Cookbook and a diet cookbook sold more than other products, the company began expanding into jewelry, media, collectibles, household products, and others.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-book-10)

### Wide Open Media publishing
By the mid-2000's, the majority of the company's revenue came from merchandise sales.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-eight-13) As late as 2019, PCH operated eight websites, including PCH Search and Win, PCH Lotto, PCH Games, PCH Save and Win, and Candystand.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Clifford-1)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-eight-13)
In 2024, direct mail and product sales were discontinued.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-57)
The Prize Patrol delivering an oversized check in 2011 to a sweepstakes winner for $1 million plus $5,000 a week for life

### Wide Open Media publishing
In 1995, PCH began the tradition of announcing winners of its $10 million prize just after the Super Bowl.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Meier-58) By the time of its bankruptcy in 2025, the company had distributed more than $500 million in prizes.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-AP-BK-2) Some of its larger prizes have been for $5,000 a week for life,[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-59) or for $10 million.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-about-60) Prizes can also range from $1 Amazon gift cards to $2,500, $1 million or $3 million.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-primary-61) The larger cash prizes are paid in installments, typically with a balloon payment at 30 years,[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-62) reducing the present value of prizes to much less than their nominal values. In August 2024, "early look" prizes were eliminated.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-63) The odds of winning "$5,000 a Week for Life" were 1 in 6.2 billion.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-64)

### Wide Open Media publishing
The Prize Patrol surprises sweepstakes winners with oversized checks for $1,000 to $10 million at their homes, workplaces, or other locations, capturing the event on video. Since their introduction in 1989, these videos have been used in widely broadcast television commercials, and, more recently, in the company's online acquisition efforts, websites and social media communications.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-resp-9)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-eight-13)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-seven-28)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-NYTTYN-65) In 2013, a $5 million television campaign modified the traditional prize patrol commercial by digitally altering video from classic sitcoms like _The Brady Bunch_ and _[Gilligan's Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilligan's\_Island "Gilligan's Island")_ to show the prize patrol visiting characters in the show.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-NYTTYN-65) Major winners are never contacted in advance; any letters, telephone calls, and social media messages claiming that a person may have already won a major prize, or claiming that they need to pay a fee to collect the prize, are always scams.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-66)

### Wide Open Media publishing
The Prize Patrol has made in-person appearances or delivered prizes on TV programs including _The Oprah Winfrey Show_,[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-67)_The Price Is Right_,[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-69) and _[Let's Make a Deal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Let's\_Make\_a\_Deal "Let's Make a Deal")_. Their surprise winning moments have been spoofed by Jay Leno,[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-70)[Conan O'Brien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conan_O'Brien "Conan O'Brien"),[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-71) and the cast of _Saturday Night Live_;[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-72) woven into the plots of movies such as _[Let's Go to Prison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Let's\_Go\_to\_Prison "Let's Go to Prison")_,[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-74)_The Sentinel_,[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-75) and _Knight and Day_;[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-76)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-77) and the TV series _Early Edition_. They have been the subject of cartoons.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-book-10)

### Government regulation and legal actions
[edit]
Beginning in the 1990s, PCH and its primary competitor, AFP, experienced a series of lawsuits claiming that their mailings misled consumers about their odds of winning and implied that magazine purchases improved their chances.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-llp-6)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-wsj-12) This led to the Deceptive Mail Prevention and Enforcement Act of 2000, which regulates direct mail businesses.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-llp-6) At the Senate hearings regarding this Act, PCH claimed most consumers were not confused about their chances of winning or that purchases did not increase their chances. The company said that fewer than five percent of participants spent more than $300.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-book-10) However, government officials from California claimed 5,000 local consumers spent more than $2,500 each in magazine purchases under the false belief that they were increasing their odds of winning the sweepstakes.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-opyltwo-18)
Industry sources estimated that PCH's response rates decreased by 7 to 12 percent and its sales volume by 22 to 30 percent in response to negative publicity from these lawsuits.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-ten-8)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-libn.com-19) In 2000, PCH laid off a quarter of its 800-person workforce.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-libn.com-19)

### Government regulation and legal actions
#### Lawsuits and settlements
[edit]
In 1992, thousands of discarded sweepstakes entries from contestants who had not bought magazine subscriptions were found in the company's trash, reinforcing beliefs that the company favored those who made purchases in selecting a sweepstakes winner.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-llp-6) PCH said this was done by a disgruntled employee at its mail processing vendor.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-book-10) A class action lawsuit ensued, which PCH settled by giving discarded entrants a second chance to win.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-llp-6)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-20)
In 1994, PCH sent mailings telling recipients they were all "finalists", which led to[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-wsj-12) a lawsuit involving the attorneys general of 14 US states.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-one-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-23) Later that year, PCH denied wrongdoing, but agreed to pay a settlement of $490,000 and to change its practices.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-one-22) Under the agreement, PCH said it would define terms like "finalist" and disclose the chances of winning.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-24)

### Government regulation and legal actions
#### Lawsuits and settlements
In 1997, a contestant of competitor AFP flew to Tampa, Florida, thinking he had won, though he had not. The resulting publicity caused more lawsuits for both companies.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-ten-8) PCH reached a $30 million national settlement in 1999.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-book-10)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-25) In 2000, another $18 million settlement was reached with 24 states, after the company sent mass mailings which said "You are a winner!" and used mock personalized checks.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-opyltwo-18)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-opyl-26) PCH agreed to avoid similar mailings in the future, and add a "sweepstakes fact box" to mailings.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-opyltwo-18)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-opyl-26)

### Wide Open Media publishing
The company's initial product was magazine subscriptions sold at a discount.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-four-53) Industry experts estimated that companies like PCH kept 75 to 90 percent of the fees from the original subscription, while publishers used the increased distribution to improve circulation numbers and revenue from renewals.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-wsj-12)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-54) PCH popularized the idea of using sweepstakes to sell magazine subscriptions through direct marketing, and became known by detractors as a producer of junk mail for advertising through mass-mailings.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Saslow-7)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-four-53) Documents filed with the New York Department of State in 1993 said that year the company mailed 220 million envelopes. Frequent buyers received 30 to 40 mailings a year.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-nine-55)
PCH began selling merchandise in 1985 with two products.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-resp-9) After a Hershey's Chocolate Cookbook and a diet cookbook sold more than other products, the company began expanding into jewelry, media, collectibles, household products, and others.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-book-10)

### Wide Open Media publishing
By the mid-2000's, the majority of the company's revenue came from merchandise sales.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-eight-13) As late as 2019, PCH operated eight websites, including PCH Search and Win, PCH Lotto, PCH Games, PCH Save and Win, and Candystand.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Clifford-1)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-eight-13)
In 2024, direct mail and product sales were discontinued.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-57)
The Prize Patrol delivering an oversized check in 2011 to a sweepstakes winner for $1 million plus $5,000 a week for life

### Wide Open Media publishing
In 1995, PCH began the tradition of announcing winners of its $10 million prize just after the Super Bowl.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-Meier-58) By the time of its bankruptcy in 2025, the company had distributed more than $500 million in prizes.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-AP-BK-2) Some of its larger prizes have been for $5,000 a week for life,[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-59) or for $10 million.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-about-60) Prizes can also range from $1 Amazon gift cards to $2,500, $1 million or $3 million.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-primary-61) The larger cash prizes are paid in installments, typically with a balloon payment at 30 years,[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-62) reducing the present value of prizes to much less than their nominal values. In August 2024, "early look" prizes were eliminated.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-63) The odds of winning "$5,000 a Week for Life" were 1 in 6.2 billion.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-64)

### Wide Open Media publishing
The Prize Patrol surprises sweepstakes winners with oversized checks for $1,000 to $10 million at their homes, workplaces, or other locations, capturing the event on video. Since their introduction in 1989, these videos have been used in widely broadcast television commercials, and, more recently, in the company's online acquisition efforts, websites and social media communications.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-resp-9)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-eight-13)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-seven-28)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-NYTTYN-65) In 2013, a $5 million television campaign modified the traditional prize patrol commercial by digitally altering video from classic sitcoms like _The Brady Bunch_ and _[Gilligan's Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilligan's\_Island "Gilligan's Island")_ to show the prize patrol visiting characters in the show.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-NYTTYN-65) Major winners are never contacted in advance; any letters, telephone calls, and social media messages claiming that a person may have already won a major prize, or claiming that they need to pay a fee to collect the prize, are always scams.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-66)

### Wide Open Media publishing
The Prize Patrol has made in-person appearances or delivered prizes on TV programs including _The Oprah Winfrey Show_,[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-67)_The Price Is Right_,[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-69) and _[Let's Make a Deal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Let's\_Make\_a\_Deal "Let's Make a Deal")_. Their surprise winning moments have been spoofed by Jay Leno,[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-70)[Conan O'Brien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conan_O'Brien "Conan O'Brien"),[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-71) and the cast of _Saturday Night Live_;[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-72) woven into the plots of movies such as _[Let's Go to Prison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Let's\_Go\_to\_Prison "Let's Go to Prison")_,[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-74)_The Sentinel_,[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-75) and _Knight and Day_;[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-76)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-77) and the TV series _Early Edition_. They have been the subject of cartoons.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Clearing_House#cite_note-book-10)
